sentences.text: Albertonykus is a member of the Alvarezsauridae family and is classified as a reptile.
It stands as the smallest known alvarezsaurid in North America, with size estimates ranging from 70 centimeters to 1.1 meters in length and a weight of 5 kilograms.
The animal possessed a small, thin head and a delicate neck supported by very long hind legs.
At just 5 kilograms, this species holds the record for the smallest alvarezsaurid discovered in North America.
Remains of this group are rarely found outside of South America and Asia, making this discovery particularly significant.
The excavation site was first located in 1910 by Barnum Brown while he searched for Albertosaurus fossils.
Over a dozen arm and leg bones of an unknown small theropod were later excavated there in 2002.
Nick Longrich identified these fossils as a new species in 2005 after comparing them to Albertosaurus claws.
The species Albertonykus borealis was formally described by Nick Longrich and Phillip Currie in 2009.
Researchers suggest the animal preyed on wood-nesting termites, a hypothesis supported by fossil wood containing typical Termopsidae termite holes found in the same formation.
The robust arm structure appears to be a specialization for excavating small holes to extract food.
Phylogenetic analysis shows Albertonykus belongs to the Asian clade Mononykini and is a sister taxon to the Asian clade Mononykinae.
The discovery of Albertonykus provides important data on the biology of Alvarezsauridae.

Albertonykus borealis lived approximately 70 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Maastrichtian stage from 72.2 to 66 million years ago, in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, Canada.
